clues.q: This Greek sky and thunder god, the child of Cronus and Rhea, rules as king of the gods on Mount Olympus.
In Norse mythology, this hammer-wielding god is associated with thunder, storms and strength.
This Olympian god presides over the sea, storms, earthquakes and horses; he had the cult title "earth shaker".
This eldest son of Cronus and Rhea is the Greek god of the dead and King of the underworld.
This Greek goddess of wisdom, warfare and handicraft was the patron of a famous city that most likely gave her its name.
This Olympian god of healing, prophecy, music, poetry and archery is the twin brother of Artemis.
Born Alcaeus, this son of Zeus and Alcmene was the greatest of the Greek heroes, famed for superhuman strength.
Anyone who looked upon this Gorgon, who had living snakes for hair, was turned to stone.
This widely revered chief god of Norse mythology has hundreds of names and titles and rides the eight-legged horse Sleipnir.
This Norse god engineers the death of the beloved god Baldr and is bound by the other gods as punishment.
This ancient Egyptian god of the Sun was believed to have ruled the sky, the Earth and the underworld.
This Egyptian god of funerary rites and guide to the underworld is usually shown as a canine or a man with a canine head.
The central character of Homer's Iliad, this son of Thetis was the greatest of all the Greek warriors of the Trojan War.
This multi-headed dog, often called the hound of Hades, guards the gates of the Greek underworld to keep the dead from leaving.
This Greek creature with the head and tail of a bull and the body of a man lived at the center of the Labyrinth on Crete.
This ancient Greek goddess of love and beauty had major cult centers at Cythera and Cyprus.
Also known as Amor, this Roman god of desire and affection is the son of Venus; his Greek counterpart is Eros.
This son of the master craftsman Daedalus was imprisoned with his father by King Minos of Crete; they escaped using wings.
In Greek myth, this first human woman was created by Hephaestus on Zeus's instructions, and each god gave her a gift.
This weapon of Norse mythology belongs to the thunder god Thor.
Aided by his winged sandals, this herald of the Greek gods protects travelers, thieves and merchants.
This son of Zeus and Hera is the Greek god of war and courage.
This Greek goddess of hunting and wild animals is the twin sister of Apollo; Diana is her Roman equivalent.
This Greek goddess of marriage, queen of the Olympians, is the sister and wife of Zeus.
This Greek god of wine-making, festivity and theatre was also called Bacchus.
This major Egyptian goddess resurrects her slain brother and husband Osiris and protects their son Horus.
This Egyptian god of the afterlife is shown partially mummy-wrapped, wearing an atef crown and holding a crook and flail.
This legendary Greek king of Ithaca, husband of Penelope and father of Telemachus, is the hero of a Homeric epic.
This son of Zeus and Danae beheaded the Gorgon Medusa and saved Andromeda from the sea monster Cetus.
This Roman god of the sky and thunder, king of the gods, was the chief deity of Roman state religion.
This Roman god of war, son of Jupiter and Juno, gave his name to the month of March.
This Roman god of the sea is the counterpart of Poseidon; his wife is Salacia.
This Roman goddess of love and beauty was claimed as an ancestor by Julius Caesar through her son Aeneas.
This Greek Titan, a champion of humankind, defied the Olympian gods by stealing fire and giving it to humanity.
In Norse mythology, this majestic hall located in Asgard is presided over by the god Odin.
This foretold series of events in Norse mythology includes a great battle, the burning of the world, and its rebirth.
After the Titanomachy, this Greek Titan was condemned to hold up the heavens for eternity.
Said to be the most beautiful woman in the world, this daughter of Zeus was first married to King Menelaus of Sparta.
This Greek hero, son of either King Aegeus of Athens or the god Poseidon, is famous for slaying the Minotaur.
This Norse goddess of love and beauty owns the necklace Brisingamen and rides a chariot pulled by two cats.
This Olympian goddess of the harvest and agriculture presides over grains and the fertility of the earth.
This Greek god of blacksmiths, metalworking and volcanoes was cast off Mount Olympus by his mother Hera because of his lameness.
This youngest of the Titans ruled during the Golden Age until he was overthrown by his son Zeus and imprisoned in Tartarus.
This Roman goddess, equated with Hera, is the wife of Jupiter and mother of Mars; her sacred animal is the peafowl.
This Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare was equated with the Greek goddess Athena.
This Roman goddess of the countryside, hunters and the Moon was born on Delos to Jupiter and Latona.
Usually shown with a two-faced head, this Roman god of beginnings, gates and doorways gave his name to January.
In Norse mythology, this location is the fortified home of the Aesir gods and is often associated with gold.
This immense sacred ash tree stands at the center of Norse cosmology, with the Nine Worlds around it.
This monstrous wolf, a child of Loki, is foretold to kill the god Odin during Ragnarok.
This Egyptian god of deserts, storms and disorder rode Ra's barque to repel the chaos serpent Apep.
This Egyptian god of the Moon, wisdom and writing was often shown with the head of an ibis or a baboon.
This Egyptian god became the patron deity of Thebes, was later joined with the sun god Ra, and had a famous oracle at Siwa Oasis.
For cheating death, this king of Ephyra was condemned to push a boulder up a hill only for it to roll back down every time.
This tragic king of Thebes unwittingly fulfilled a prophecy that he would kill his father; his story was told by Sophocles.
This legendary Thracian musician sailed with the Argonauts and descended into the underworld to bring back his wife Eurydice.
This Greek hero, son of Aeson of Iolcos and husband of Medea, led the Argonauts on a quest for the Golden Fleece.
This serpentine lake monster of Greek myth made its lair in the lake of Lerna, said to be an entrance to the Underworld.
This Norse god, son of Odin and Frigg and brother of Thor, is killed through a scheme by Loki.
Called the best of all horses, this eight-legged steed of Norse mythology is ridden by Odin.
This major Egyptian sky goddess, mother or consort of Horus and Ra, was one of the goddesses who acted as the Eye of Ra.
This Egyptian god associated with pharaonic power is usually shown as a Nile crocodile or a crocodile-headed man.
This Egyptian creator god and patron of craftsmen and architects is the husband of Sekhmet in the triad of Memphis.
This Egyptian warrior goddess of medicine, called "the eye of Ra", is associated with Hathor and Bastet.
This Egyptian goddess personified truth, balance, law and justice; her opposite was Isfet.
This Egyptian goddess of the sky, wife of Geb, was the mother of Osiris, Set, Isis and Nephthys.
This Egyptian god of the Earth was believed to cause earthquakes with his laughter.
This keen-eyed Norse god keeps watch for invaders and the onset of Ragnarok where the rainbow bridge Bifrost meets the sky.
This Norse god sacrificed his right hand to the wolf Fenrir, who bit it off when he realized he had been bound.
Also called the World Serpent, this huge Norse sea serpent encircles the Earth while biting its own tail.
In Norse mythology, this burning rainbow bridge reaches between Midgard and Asgard.
This female being in Norse mythology presides over an underworld realm of the same name, where she receives a portion of the dead.
This Trojan priestess was fated by Apollo to utter true prophecies but never to be believed.
This witch and goddess, daughter of the sun god Helios, used potions and herbs to transform her enemies into animals.
This sorceress, daughter of King Aeetes of Colchis and niece of Circe, was the wife of Jason.
This Greek ferryman carries the souls of the dead across the river bordering the underworld; coins were left for him in burials.
In Ovid's version of her tale, this talented mortal challenged the goddess Minerva to a weaving contest.
This Roman god of fire and the forge, the counterpart of Hephaestus, was honored at a festival held every August 23.
This Roman goddess of luck, whose Greek equivalent is Tyche, was often shown with a wheel and a horn of plenty.
This man-eating Greek monster lived on one side of a narrow strait, opposite the whirlpools of Charybdis.
This Egyptian deity of chaos and darkness, the opponent of Ra and of Maat, was usually shown as a giant serpent.
This scarab-faced Egyptian god represents the rising or morning sun.
This Egyptian protective goddess of childbirth, whose name means "great one", was shown as a female hippopotamus.
Often shown as a bearded dwarf, this Egyptian household god was worshipped as a protector of mothers and children.
This Egyptian goddess with a crocodile head, lion forequarters and hippo hindquarters played a role in the Judgment of the Dead.
This Norse figure renowned for wisdom was beheaded in the Aesir-Vanir War; Odin carries his head, which counsels him.
This Norse goddess associated with apples and youth is the wife of the poet god Bragi.
In Snorri's Prose Edda, he is the Norse god of poetry, renowned for eloquence among the gods.
This Norse jotunn and goddess is associated with bowhunting, skiing, winter and mountains.
This Norse jotunn guards Muspelheim, one of only two realms that existed before the beginning of time.
In Norse mythology, this is the primordial, magical void described in the Gylfaginning's account of creation.
This Norse jotunn personifies the sea, hosts the gods in his halls, and is associated with brewing ale.
This Norse goddess associated with the earth is known for her golden hair and is married to the thunder god Thor.
This Roman goddess of war, wearing a military helmet, rides into battle in a four-horse chariot.
This Roman goddess of fruitful abundance gets her name from the Latin word for orchard fruit.
This blind prophet of Apollo in Thebes served as an advisor to Cadmus, the city's founder.
This Greek bandit from Attica forced his victims to fit the size of an iron bed by stretching them or cutting their legs.
In Tartarus, this Greek figure stands in a pool beneath a fruit tree, but the fruit and water always stay out of reach.
This many-eyed giant served Hera as a watchman, guarding Io after Zeus turned her into a heifer.
In Greek mythology, this man of bronze protected Crete from pirates and invaders.
